utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again. We still have to deal with certain issues but, Mr. Ierace, I think the whole day was scheduled for Witness Y.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it was anticipated that Witness Y would finish either yesterday or this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The next witness is Mr. Mole, the unfortunate Mr. Mole, because he has come twice before, already given evidence in two parts in evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore, I would be anxious to complete him, since not only is his evidence in chief already to have been in three parts, but he has spend weeks, rather than days, sitting around waiting to give evidence on past occasions. Could I respectfully suggest that we at least complete evidence in chief of Mr. Mole? However, I am conscious of time constraints, and if the break could happen before 10.30, I wish to revise the list of exhibits in order to keep his evidence in chief as very brief as possible. But, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We have a few other issues as well. We still have the 92 bis statements which we should hear the parties upon. It was already indicated it should be done on Thursday or on Friday. We can't leave that forever. So I would prefer to start with that, but let's just first hear Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, regarding 92 bis, I am still waiting for the answers from the Prosecution. We said, so that we can give our position, we have to have access to this pile of documents that you may have received already. What we received is for part important, that is important, is not legible because of bad copies and so on. I have written to the Prosecution asking if we can have something that was legible and visible, and we are still expecting an answer. I really can't go any further until the Prosecution has answered and brought us some copies that are clear and legible. Therefore, we cannot give our position until the Prosecution has done its part of the job.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I don't recall that letter. Either it was so long ago that we have dealt with it and I have put it out of my mind or we have not received it. So perhaps during the break my friend can give me a copy of it and I will check to see what's been done. Also on 92 bis, I think last week, Mr. President, you asked that we do certain things in relation to the material. We will check during the break that those things have been done. Certainly, there are some outstanding matters. There is also the matter of the expert witnesses, one of whom is to give evidence this Friday, hopefully. So perhaps in terms of 92 bis, my friend could clarify his concern with us over the first break and we can perhaps at least sort that out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When you are talking about the expert witnesses, you are talking about the experts Philips and Tabeau, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The decision will be given in due time as far as it's not already very late. I have one question for the Defence at this very moment. 92 bis under (E) says that "A party seeking to adduce a written statement or transcript shall give fourteen days notice to the opposing party, who may within seven days object." Is it true that no objection has been filed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that no objection has been made in writing, but verbally, our position has been clearly stated and I think that everyone knows this. I don't think that the text makes it necessary for it to be a written objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...please tell us what your objections are about, apart from parts of the documents being illegible.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you want us to state our position now? I am not ready. I am going to have a look at it, and perhaps after the break I would give you our position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence was requested to prepare for that by last Thursday or Friday, and I know it is Tuesday now. And I also would like to know because there was an objection filed at the previous occasion of filing documents, but since that filing was withdrawn, the Chamber wondered whether or not you considered that filing of objections to be a repeated or -- it is unclear to us at this very moment what the position of the Defence is. And we would like to know that so that we can take decisions. If you say you can't do it now, then perhaps we could use the remaining five minutes --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I can do, unless you want to pass a -- take a decision now, is that I can draft the position - perhaps it would be clearer for everyone - the position of the Defence, The chronology of the events and then you can have it by tonight or this afternoon, then you can have it directly in writing. Perhaps that would be the best thing to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will consider that during the break, whether this would be a solution. I don't know whether the Prosecution would oppose against such a filing, at least such written communication, in respect of 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Leaving to one side the issue of whether the Defence has precluded itself by not complying with the filing timetable, I would have no objection, Mr. President. There is also the matter of the report of the Mr. Zarkovic [sic]. I appreciate there are outstanding matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I was waiting, as a matter of fact, for Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He arrived expectantly with five minutes to go yesterday afternoon, but we did not get to him. I assume you mean Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Is Mr. Stamp there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: He was here yesterday afternoon. He is not here at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I would have expected that he would give the answers. Perhaps I could -- the question I would like to put to him is that since there are two parts of the report that bear no signature at all, just written text, typewritten text -- well, as far as I do understand the Defence, could have been produced by anyone. On the other hand, I noticed that, I would say, almost everything that would be in that part of the text was dealt with during the examination of the witness. So I wondered whether the Prosecution intended to argue on whether or not signatures are needed for those specific two, I would say, further elaborations of the report or that they would say, well, since this has all been dealt with in the examination of the expert, we could also do without. That would have been my question to Mr. Stamp.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We will forward the question, Mr. President, and he can attend at a time to suit your convenience, either immediately after the break or perhaps before 1.45.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If you -- yes. We have to consider at what time we will deal with the matter. Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Since you said "Madam Pilipovic" would also be fine, I leave it up to you whether I should change the way I address you. I would be glad to do so.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour. As for the position of the Defence regarding the motion which was given to the Defence on the 29th of January, 2002, concerning the introduction of evidence pursuant to 92 bis, we gave our position on the 4th of February, 2002. In that response, we elaborated our objection to the introduction of evidence pursuant to 92 bis. We stated our position in respect of every witness individually, that is the witnesses in respect of whom the Prosecution was availing themselves to the 92 bis. After we received the document on the 6th of June, that is the motion of the 6th of June, 2001, which motion withdrew two statements. I believe one of them was the Krestalica statement and I don't remember at this point the other one. We were once again on that occasion given the material which was also given to us for the first time on the 29th of January. For these reasons, because we believe that we had already stated our position regarding this material and the statements in question, we did not feel the need to state our objection once again because the documents in question were one and the same documents. So we still abide by our position. And if it is necessary for the purposes of your decision, Your Honour, we can state once again our response to the motion regarding the evidence pursuant to 92 bis or we can put it in writing once again during the break or in the afternoon; or we can also, after the break, briefly explain once again why we object to the introduction of evidence pursuant to 92 bis as it has been proposed by my learned colleagues. Likewise, we would like to address the issue of the statement of the late Hamdija Cavcic, after the decision was reached by the Appeals Chamber on the 7th of June, 2002.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand. That is a -- I would say a separate issue that is 92 bis (C). But this is exactly the kind of clarification the Chamber was seeking, whether the objections filed at an earlier occasion would still stand as to the objection against the documents that were filed again by the Prosecution. So the only question that then remains is whether there are any --

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- And then of course we would have to consider whether any additional objections should have been filed or not. Rule 92 bis also says that the parties should be heard. If there are any additional objections, please prepare to explain them briefly to the Chamber. We will then adjourn until 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am glad to see that you are back. It -- your testimony is cut into small pieces until now, which we regret, but sometimes we have no choice. Thank you, therefore, for coming back. Mr. Ierace, I think you had not yet finished the examination-in-chief, so would you please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. Mole, good morning.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the last occasion that you were here, you told us that there was a perception that events elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina impacted literally on Sarajevo in that the city would be shelled indiscriminately. Do you remember saying that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President I have to ask Mr. Ierace if he could quote the exact reference in the preceding statement of Mr. Mole.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It has been a very long time, Mr. Ierace. So if you could find the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In LiveNote, it is page 9827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you have a date, perhaps, first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. It is the 1st of July and that is the page number --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 1st of July?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The 7th of June would be a --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 7th of June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- would be a better idea. And then it would be page?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Page 9827.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, appears that at least --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Line 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 9827. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will read the answer to remove any doubt. Do you remember telling us this: "There was an accepted norm that if the Serb side failed to achieve their objectives, and I use that in the wider context, so that could be anything from a local complaint to something else that happened within Bosnia, the general perception was that Sarajevo would suffer as a result. This was always interpreted to mean that artillery fire would be brought to bear on the city in response."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are just reading. Let's first --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not have the same references as you do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you listen carefully, you will check whether it a literal reading and I will assist you then. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "There were instances where this was quite specifically made as a threat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, you -- don't you have LiveNote on your computer?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have it, perhaps, but I took the hard copy and on page 9, 8279, it was me addressing to you a question. So I don't know if the reference given by Mr. Ierace is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is page 9827, English version, line 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well then. I will look it up on my computer.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We have a spare copy for my learned colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would assist you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That we have, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, did you share that general perception?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And you said there were instances where this was quite specifically made as a threat. Was it ever made as a threat to you by General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was made as a threat both individually by General Galic as well as from Serb liaison officers which we had in the PTT building.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Can you recollect any examples of General Galic making such a threat to you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detailed instances would be noted in the two statements that I have made with the dates. We have already, in my previous evidence, identified that 10 years later specific dates are hard for me to recall from memory, but there was a general perception that other events within Bosnia were key pressure points which, if events were not going according to the Serb side's plans, the city of Sarajevo, which was to all intents and purposes in a hostage situation, would be used as a counter pressure point for the events elsewhere in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And I think indeed you have already given that evidence. If I can ask you to focus on the particular questions. I think essentially you are saying you don't recall a specific instances at this stage without the assistance of documents. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct. But I remember certain pressure points where what I have outlined did occur. For example, Brcko was a pressure point which was mentioned frequently.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: By General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That I don't remember. I believe there was a place, Trebinje - I think I have that in my statement - where reverses had occurred which caused a threat to be applied to other cities beside Sarajevo. Zagreb, I recall being one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Again, was that by General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: To you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, did it reach the point where you became something of a student as to what was happening elsewhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: One would be foolish in the situation that I found myself in not to pay full attention to the events elsewhere in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: As a result of your anticipation of events elsewhere in Bosnia and the possible impact on Sarajevo, did you ever take any steps to pre-empt attacks on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whenever we in our briefings in each morning in the sector were notified that events elsewhere in Bosnia had progressed one way or the other, we would then be alerted to the possibility of repercussions within our sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And did you ever, in those circumstances, take any steps in order to pre-empt attacks on Sarajevo? Did you ever send any messages, perhaps, anything of that nature?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We would respond to complaints and observations from both sides, and that would be the means by which we would then take action.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps I am not making myself clear. I am not talking about responses to attacks on the city which have already taken place but rather if you observed that things were going badly for the Serb forces elsewhere in Bosnia, given that pattern that you told us about, did you ever seek to step in before there were retaliatory attacks on Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand. Because our meetings were frequent, these events would be part of discussion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And discussion with whom?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With General Galic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, to be specific, did you make clear to him that you didn't want retaliatory action on Sarajevo as a result of Serb setbacks elsewhere in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be included in the conversation, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, before I take you to some documents, while you were in Sarajevo, did General Galic receive a promotion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: From what rank to what rank?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Colonel to General.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: When was that, approximately?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: November 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever discuss that with General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I congratulated him on his promotion.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did he ever explain to you why he understood he was being promoted?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just regarding the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Speaking the same language, I must have -- I must ask you to slow down a bit. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I suppose this is trite to state, but is it the case in military structures that one is promoted when one is perceived by their superiors to be doing well?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but one would obviously have to condition that with which activities had been seen to have been performed to such an extent that promotion was granted. It could well have been from before the appearance of Colonel, then General, Galic in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I would like to ask you some questions about some other individuals in the Sarajevo Romanija Corps. Colonel Zarkovic, did you ever meet him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was his position, as you recollect it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, one would have to consider all the statements that I have made --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you don't remember, then that is fine. Just tell us.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Although you don't remember his position, do you remember anything of his general attitude in terms of whether he took a soft line, a medium line, or whatever, by comparison to General Galic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my dealings with that individual, he was a reasonable, intelligent and understanding person who would be of moderate views, generally.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: How did that compare to General Galic's position, in a general sense?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought that General Galic was much harder of line, more dedicated of purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Colonel Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we are making the same comparison in terms of character, are we?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: No, just what position did he have in the SRK, as you recollect it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, I didn't get the name of the individual in question, and secondly, I have to object for reasons of relevance. I don't know how all these names can be relevant to the case against General Galic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you please respond to the relevance issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is part of the establishing the texture of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps, in other words, senior subordinates to General Galic. You may recall there has been evidence already as to some critical conversations with Colonel Zarkovic from other witnesses. And it is therefore appropriate to bring out where he was in the structure and his general attitude compared to that of the accused so as to provide more of a context from -- for the earlier conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That is the first comparison you asked the witness to make, I think, because you now say Colonel -- that is not clearly in my mind. That is the second --

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Kosovac, yes. And I don't seek a comparison between him and General Galic in that sense. I propose to ask the witness if he recollects the positions of Colonel Kosovac and two others

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you are not putting the same question to him. Yes. So if you would then please repeat your question. The name has become clear to you now, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I take it. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect meeting a Colonel Kosovac?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the name is still not clear. I think I heard the word Kosovac but I am not sure. Could my learned colleague spell it out so that we have it clear on the record. Secondly, the objection still stands to the extent that we do not see how this witness can establish the structure of the Romanija Corps. I don't think that that is the purpose of this testimony. Even if it is, I don't know how this witness can assist us in this respect.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, the names of these people appear on page 8 of the statement of the witness, taken on the 3rd of September 1997. I'm surprised that my friend --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the surprise is quite clear. If the statement is in the hands, it is just for the Chamber perhaps of some importance. I take it that it will be dealt with overnight. Yes, please. And then the second issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I respectfully submit it is obvious that when an accused is charged with command responsibility, that it makes perfect sense to lead evidence as to his senior subordinates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The objection is denied. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect whether Colonel Kosovac was relatively high or low in the command structure for the Sarajevo Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In relative terms, he was high in that structure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Colonel Pasic, do you recollect meeting him?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you recollect his position?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I recollected his position when I gave my statement in 1997. Further, five years have passed by so I would rather my statement stood. I can't remember sitting here now.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And finally, Vladimir Lukic?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Same applies.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, were there -- I think you referred to daily meetings or at least meetings earlier this morning at which information would be provided within the UN structure. Were there daily meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What part of the UN structure would conduct those meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The United Nations presence in Sarajevo was a sector. That sector had a headquarters and three battalions under command. Within that structure and that headquarters, alongside the operations room of the sector was the UNMO, UNMO organisation. The operations room of the sector would have a morning "O" group, operations group meeting, and I would have similar meetings in the evening with my senior officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If I could summarise that evidence, are you saying that, each morning, the operations unit conducted a meeting and, each evening, you conducted a meeting for the UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you attend the morning meetings?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always I attended those meetings and had the opportunity to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear it said at either an operation unit meeting or the daily UNMO meetings that a United Nations investigation had established that the source of fire of a shelling incident which occurred within the territory controlled by the Bosnian government was also within the territory controlled by the Bosnian government? In other words, did you ever hear it said that a United Nations investigation had established as a fact that Bosnian forces had fired on their own civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Ms. Pilipovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I don't think I fully understand what incident we are talking about. Could my learned colleague be more precise, please, and give us the time framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, could you please respond to it, although am I right in understanding that you are talking in rather general terms but within the time period when the witness was in Sarajevo, I take it?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because otherwise he couldn't have heard anything over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please answer the question. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand what you are asking. There was a general perception that the Presidency side would benefit more on the global scale if they were perceived to be the beleaguered party. To maintain that image, I am sure - though I cannot give evidence of fact - that incidents occurred where, to perpetuate that beleaguered viewpoint and to increase the possibility of outside involvement from NATO and other outside agencies, that the Presidency forces may well have fired upon their own city to maintain that beleaguered viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, would you please focus on the wording of the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think I have to intervene now. The word "beleagured" party is not in the transcript, but I think we have all heard it by now. Could the witness please repeat it for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps the witness could read the answer on the screen, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 19.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Mole, could you please look at page 50, line 19, which is approximately in the middle of your screen. Did you say, "perceived to be the beleaguered party"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. For the French booth, the word in question was "assieger," beleaguered, and not "belligerant," belligerent.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You say that they may well have fired upon their own city. Sir, what I am asking is whether you are aware of any UN report conducted into any incident during the time that you were in Sarajevo which established that as a fact?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Remembering that the task of the UNMO group was not to investigate in a police fashion the events to which we refer, I can only tell you that there were incidents which were investigated and we understand that there was an element of doubt as to the origin of the fire that had done the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I ask the witness be shown -- I withdraw that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Just some other brief questions. Are you aware as to whether the Serb forces had access to United Nations communications, in other words, the ability to listen in to communications, for instance, between UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did. The liaison officers which were appointed by the sector and were located in the PTT building had difficulty connecting with their side outside the city, as telephone communications were in doubt. As a result, we provided, that is, the United Nations provided, communications facility for them to fulfill their task.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, given the time is very brief, if you could answer the questions properly with a "yes" or "no," perhaps you could do that. Just to assist you in order to overcome that problem, did you provide a piece of equipment to them?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What was the type of equipment?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A Motorola.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Was that the type of equipment used by UNMOs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did that give them the ability to listen in to UNMO conversations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you ever see staff of the Sarajevo Romanija Corps with Motorolas?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, you told us on an earlier occasion that you travelled around the front line one day. What was the approximate length of the front line around the city?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: 64 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: During your time in Sarajevo, what were the mortar sizes used by the Serb forces, the Serb army forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anything from 6-inch mortar to 122-millimetre mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Did you personally see mortars of the size of approximately 122 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: On the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you know whether the Bosnian government forces had mortars of a similar size?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I really have to object to this question. A mortar does not have approximately 122, 60, 80 or so millimetres. We are talking about very exact calibres and we know what calibres are we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, would you please respond to the objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, it is a proper question. I am aware of what the issue is which is operating in my friend's mind, and I am sure that if I was to ask a leading question on it, he would be the first to object. But I am happy to do that. Perhaps he can object if he doesn't like the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you sure the mortars were 122 millimetres exactly, or were they another size?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many sizes. That one would be included.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What I'm essentially asking is: Was it exactly 122 or 124 or 118 or some similar size that was used by the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now coming back to my following question: Do you know whether the Bosnian government forces had mortars of a similar size to 122 millimetres?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I ask the witness be shown some documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you please assist, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 354 is the first.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does the document you have just been handed appear to be a photocopy of a daily sit-rep from you to Zagreb headquarters?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I direct your attention firstly to the date. Is that the 20th of October, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I now direct your attention to paragraph 3 on page 1, and under the heading "continuous affairs," do you refer to an incident the previous day when police forces on the Serbian side took," to use your words, "great exception to workers from Presidency area on mission," in relation to some water repairs?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you relate that the Serbian police intended to arrest the workers -- I will read on, quoting: "But only armed intervention by Serb liaison officer and his guards with mission prevented this occurrence. Once again, this provides a clear indication that there is not a well-coordinated and unified command structure on either side." Does that appear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to that incident --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The French interpreter asks Mr. Ierace to repeat the last question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that appear?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, the French booth has a sort of a little bit of a problem. Could Mr. Ierace repeat the last question, please, and the quotation?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Was that half the question in relation to that incident or already the question: "Do you relate relating that the Serbian police ..."?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In relation to that question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please repeat that, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: That is the whole question, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President now, we are at it, and since I have the document in front of us, may I ask Mr. Ierace to apply the same rule as it applies to me and to quote the whole sentence and not just a portion of the text that he has picked out. Says the quotation that I see in the record starts with a "but" if I am not mistaken. Previous page, line 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, we have extreme time concerns. I withdraw the question. Might the document be returned, and I ask the witness be given Exhibit 3689?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, was it the case that monthly reports were prepared summarising the events, mostly on a daily basis, which had occurred over that month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In many cases, would the entries in the monthly report come from the daily sit-reps?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have before you the senior military observer's end of the month report for October?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President. Mr. President, this document will have to be dealt with in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We will then turn into closed session. I see it bears an "R" number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [redacted

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session again.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have before you a copy of your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. What is the witness supposed to have in front of him? I think you said that the next document which was not identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I am definitely speeding up too much, Mr. President. Exhibit 358.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, in order to respect the quality, could Mr. Ierace please repeat the number which is only appearing now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't understand, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have it in front of you with the number on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It was not appearing in the transcript when I started my intervention. That is why I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, that is what I just indicated. It clearly is in the transcript. If you start intervening when the -- those who are responsible for the transcript have not even been able to identify an issue, if you have the document in front of you, just wait and see whether we all have the same document in front of us, and if it does not appear in the transcript, the tiny yellow paper will do. Do not interfere and intervene at a too early stage.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I did not have a document before me. I was looking in my folder without a reference. I did not have a document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The document showed to the witness always are distributed. So even if you would not have had it in front of you at that very -- I wouldn't say minute but at that very second, it would have been there in five seconds. That is exactly what I am asking you to do, is to first see what happens, unless there is very technical objection, and not intervene unnecessarily.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. President the reference in page 62, line 22, and it is the exact reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to the entry for the 7th of November -- sorry. Yes, the 7th of November. Is this the second sentence: "General alert declared by Presidency in city in response to Serb threat of dire consequences if the approximately 6.000 refugees were not allowed to leave the city by 1400 hours today"? Does that appear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. And does the balance of the entry make clear that the refugees included apparently some Croatian people who wanted to travel to Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you now go to the entry for the 8th of November -- I withdraw that. Is that another example of a threat -- I withdraw that. Would you please go to the following day's entry, in particular over the page, the first line: "Yesterday's threat by Serbs to Presidency of dire consequences if the approximately 6.000 refugees were not allowed to leave the city were apparently not followed through in any large measure, although general shelling activity somewhat heavier today." Do you see that entry?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do those two entries, that is for the 7th and 8th, illustrate again that same pattern of threatening the use of indiscriminate fire if the political or other objectives of the Serb forces were not met?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It does. And the second incident was one I referred to about half an hour ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Indeed. Do you mean the words which immediately follow on from where I stopped quoting?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It relates to the Croatian attack on Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I'll come to that now. Does the entry go on to read, "At approximately 900 hours, received message from Serbian liaison GP at Lukavica concerning Croatian attack on ... " And perhaps you could pronounce that word.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nevesinje.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "[Approximately 24 kilometres south-east of Mostar] Serbs indicated that six villages had already been burnt. Serbs threatened that if attack did not cease by 1100 hours, that they would reply by shelling Dubrovnik, Slavonski Brod, Cantat and Zagreb. As requested, message was passed to General Morillon who was in the sector headquarters and he dealt with it from there."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I object again in relation to the areas, to the territories, which are not covered by the indictment. This is the same kind of objection that I made in relation to Breza and Zupca and now in relation to Dubrovnik and Slavonski Brod. So really, General Galic did not have any kind of authority. It was nothing to do with his corps of the army. So if we are going to look at the behaviour of third parties, of nothing to do with the other corps, if we are going to align them with the person of General Galic, this is not what the Defence can accept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, my next question was going to be, in view of his earlier evidence, whether he has any understanding of General Galic being involved in that threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I will apologise but this is very difficult thing to swallow. We know very well that General Galic had nothing to do with Dubrovnik. We know that very well, but I think that we are wasting time and we are going to waste a lot of time. The position of the Defence is to reiterate this position. We are only interested in Sarajevo according to what is written in the indictment. Why are we now going to be asking questions about Dubrovnik? Dubrovnik, let us remind ourselves, is many kilometres away from Sarajevo, and it is not admissible fundamentally and specifically. And not even to speak about Zagreb because Zagreb was even mentioned last time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Even without this mentioning of Zagreb, the objection was clear to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer to discuss further the matter the objection during the break. If it would be possible for you, Mr. Ierace, to touch on a different subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Could I briefly respond to my friend's concern so that you will have the benefit of that argument during the break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware that now and then I am perhaps too quick in consulting my colleagues rather than first listen better to the parties. I apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is necessary, I think, to clarify with the witness what involvement, if any, General Galic had within that threat as he understands it because of the witness's earlier evidence, which the witness himself has referred to --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we going to be speaking of this before the witness? That is what I want to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...not of everything, perhaps, but I am carefully listening to Mr. Ierace, and I take it that usually the parties, if they touch ground of which they think it would be better to discuss the matter in the absence of the witness, they will ask the Chamber. And the Chamber is very alert on that as well. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. You recall that the witness, in fact, drew the attention to the Trial Chamber to this entry in the document and said words to the effect, "This is something I was talking about earlier," something like that. Earlier, I had asked him of instances of threats regarding General Galic. Accepting for the sake of the argument that the witness -- that there is no connection, the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. relevance is, firstly, the background of other evidence that Sarajevo was a lever in the Bosnia-wide context. The second point of relevance is that the threat emanated from the Serb liaison officer at Lukavica, which has obvious significance. In other words, to the extent that General Galic, according to this witness's evidence, was instrumental in threatening action against Sarajevo in order to achieve Bosnia-wide objectives, this one coming through Lukavica further makes clear the role of Lukavica in at least a communication point for these coordinated connections between events. Thank you, Mr. President. That is all I wish to say on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would you then -- yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when we start after the next break, the Defence would clearly like to make an intervention following by what the Prosecution just spoke before the witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps to have just before the break so that we can consider whatever you have to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, but then I have to do it in the absence of the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Mr. Ierace, would you please take care that a couple of minutes before we start the break that you interrupt the examination-in-chief and ask the witness then, not now, to leave the courtroom before we have the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, the next entry is the 22nd of November.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, just to be very precise and very clear, I have to indicate now that the Defence believes that its rights have been offended and one of the positions that I am going to explain later, I now have to make a general observation, is that this way of proceeding is offending the rights of the Defence. I will explain a little later. And I don't think the follow-up testimony should be possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I take it that you touch upon a different subject now. Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, in relation to the entry for the 22nd of November 1992, did you note that there was a high level of activity with 192 rounds incoming to the Presidency side and two rounds incoming to the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you read four lines down, do these words appear: "Today, General Morillon requested an update on the activity in the sector, and when appraised of the heavy shelling into the city, directed that the Serbs be asked the reason for this activity. When asked, the Serbs answered that the shelling was in response to a mid-morning attack by Presidency forces against Hresa," spelled H-r-e-s-a, "grid 4058. The attack was said to have been made by infantry supported by hand-held anti-tank weapons. Furthermore, they indicated that the artillery then followed the retreating forces back into the city. It should be noted that the UNMO position observing Hresa was unaware of any infantry attacks to the area. Furthermore, the pattern of shelling by the Serbs did not indicate a specific operation in support of forces in Hresa but was widely spread throughout the city. Shelling into the city still continues at the time of writing of this report." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is the city referred to Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is this another example of the relationship between -- I withdraw that. Essentially, you seem to be saying in that entry that the explanation provided by the representatives of the Serb forces was quite inconsistent with your own independent observations by the UNMOs. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is absolutely true.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. I am up because I believe that this is a leading question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It is a leading question, Mr. President, and it is leading in the sense that it summarises quite fairly, I would suggest, what the passage says, and I have taken the step of reading the passage out. Therefore, although leading, it is not, in my respectful submission, objectionable for that reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The objection is denied. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Might that document be returned. Might the witness be shown document 511.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, is this a memorandum from you to the Sector Commander dated the 11th of December, 1992, on the subject of an upsurge in violence, to use the subheading, between the 1st and 10th of December, 1992?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to paragraph 12 which is on the second page. I draw your attention to about the third sentence at paragraph 12, approximately four lines down. Indeed, six lines down. "The Serbs still maintain their pressure on the city by an occasional random round or two into the city and no noticeable change in activity level from before the ceasefire on the periphery of the city." The observation you made there of "an occasional random round or two into the city," with what frequently did that type of shelling pattern occur?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I am indicating is the random shelling which we became familiar with daily throughout my tour did not vary necessarily according to military objectives. So in specific answer to your question, this brief relates to a particular conflict, but my indication in paragraph 12 shows that the random shelling in the city was not related to military objectives related to in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, might that document we returned. And would this be a convenient time?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher, may I ask you to escort Mr. Mole out of the courtroom, since we have to deal with the procedural matter in your absence, Mr. Mole. I take it that we will resume at 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, the sequence of events that happened earlier was perhaps a demonstration that sometimes rapidity doesn't serve us well. What I asked was that the witness leaves and my advice wasn't followed, but never mind. But what we want to raise is an objection of principle. Why? Because this witness was not interrogated in a normal way, examined in a certain way. Simply, the Prosecution pleaded before the witness not to ask him questions but of such grave things, serious things, for the accused, like the Lukavica had a very important role in the organisation and coordination of all the other events as distinct that we know, that we should know, in Sarajevo and those in Dubrovnik. Now, the Prosecution gave us a thesis here, a version, it clearly stated before the witness that Lukavica or General Galic was nothing else but responsible for this connection of these events on various levels. Consequently, not asking questions by stating it here officially and publicly before the witness, the Prosecution has obviously put the witness in a position of being biased. No matter -- however we look at the problem, they have made him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me ask you one thing, Mr. Piletta-Zanin. Would it be possible that the Prosecution summarised what is essentially the content of the entry on the 8th of November, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I had the impression here not of a summary. We were told a lot more in what Mr. Ierace said than just the entry that you mentioned. I think what is here being entered into evidence is the personal responsibility of General Galic in the framework of the events that took place in Dubrovnik and Sarajevo as being a machine that General Galic was responsible for. That was more or less the thesis by the Prosecution, and the Prosecution obviously stated this and put General Galic in Lukavica, exposed them as such. And on one hand, we are here outside the territorial framework of the indictment, and on the other hand, we are here stating things in front of the witness and his testimony hasn't finished yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Very quickly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At no stage did I suggest that General Galic had personal responsibility for events in Dubrovnik. This is the document of the witness. I have said nothing in my submissions which is not, in fact, the evidence of this witness already and that is why I did not ask that the witness be taken from the courtroom. The issue is simply that the witness himself has, on the face of the -- his evidence, drawn a connection between General Galic and this incident, at least potentially, by saying, not in response to any question from me, that this aspect of his report is what he was referring to earlier in his evidence. What I seek to do is to ask him if there is a connection and if indeed General Galic was involved in the conveyance of this threat. Assuming that his answer is, on reflection, no, General Galic was not involved with this particular incident, it still has relevance to the Prosecution case because it comes through Lukavica and simply makes the point that the evidence of this witness and others to the effect that General Galic threatened to indiscriminately fire against Sarajevo, if events did not work out according to the wishes of the Serb forces elsewhere in Bosnia, that his forward headquarters, to use the words of the Defence, were where this threat came from. In other words, that threats in relation to events elsewhere in Bosnia which involved action against places elsewhere in Bosnia also came through Lukavica, at least on this one instance. To emphasise my point, I am not saying that General Galic is responsible for events that took place in Dubrovnik. It is not part of this indictment to explore what General Galic did beyond Sarajevo in this time frame. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I can see that at the same time that Mr. Ierace is saying that General Galic is not responsible of this, he is saying that Lukavica is, and this is exactly where the problem lies. This is here just a synonym, really, a metonymy, really.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...until 10 minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: As far as the objection by the Defence is concerned, the alleged threats the document P358 is about are directly related to the Croatian-Serbian armed conflict, at quite a distance from Sarajevo, and relates to retaliation against cities that are similarly far away from Sarajevo, and Dubrovnik, Slavonski Brod, Zagreb, all on Croatian territory. I did not mention Cantat because the Chamber had not enough time to identify whether Cantat is also on Croatian territory. If it is, then it would even strengthen the reasoning of this decision. Therefore, the Chamber considers that the possible Lukavica involvement in passing the alleged threats not of assistance for the determination of its decision it has to make. Therefore, the objection is sustained. The witness may be brought in again.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. If we can perhaps ask the witness to remain outside for perhaps 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...unfortunately, Mr. Piletta-Zanin only asked me to have another 30 seconds in your absence when you were already in the courtroom. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In quizzes, they say: Your 30 seconds have started now, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Briefly, our objection was that in view of the allegations of the Prosecution in the framework of this witness, this was something very similar to what has already been prohibited by the Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the interpretation, I was not speaking of anything that should have been prohibited by the Chamber. I am sorry. I was referring to a principle. It is prohibited to make contact during the examination with the witness in order to explain what the position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I am not quite sure that I followed you. Let me just read for one second. In English, you say: "It is prohibited to make contact with the witness during the examination in order to explain what the position is." It is not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. What I said before the break, Mr. President, is the following: The fact for the Prosecution to have actually pleaded in front of the witness and to have exposed their position has, to a certain effect, pre-formed, generally speaking, the witness for the examination. So it is the same as making contact with the witness during the examination, which is not permissible. Since the Prosecution has decided to proceed in this way, this witness has to a certain extent now been tainted because of this way of proceeding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, if one would accept your reasoning, then it would certainly be limited to the subject and not in general contaminate this witness. I stress, "if" you would have already followed that. Therefore, the Prosecution may continue to examine the witness. Could you please bring in the witness, Madam Usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Might the witness be shown Exhibit 618.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Sir, do you have before you the Senior Military Observer's end of month report for December?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have told us that you were relieved by Lieutenant Colonel Cutler at the end of December, I think around the 25th or 26th. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Therefore, his signature appears on the report on the last page. Is that so?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In fact, the entries up until the changeover date reflect your period. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And does that part of the report essentially constitute your portion of it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, you have told us that in the first 10 days or so of December, there was fierce fighting in the area of Otes. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: You have also told us that there was a very high number of shells that landed on the Sarajevan side during that battle. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the area of Otes, I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, I will firstly take you to a number of references in the report on various days in relation to whether there was shelling elsewhere in the city during that period. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In that context, firstly, I take you to the entry for the 5th of December, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. PILIPOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. I have a technical problem. Exhibit 618, pursuant to the documents that have been provided by the Prosecution, is 620, in order to avoid any confusion. We are talking about the monthly report for the month of December as Exhibit number 620 and not 618. The problem concerns only the numbering, so that we should not be misled later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have in front of me P618, which starts at the bottom 00411996.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President, but the problem is that this document was disclosed, at least that is what it seems, for the same period of time under number 620 and I think that we have exactly the same copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the number just indicated by me as the ERN number at the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the document that we have now, yes. But not on 620, which is the same document. I don't know if we risk having any problems because of this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, is the last page, last three digits 008?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Meanwhile, the other pages are there as well. But that is now document P618 the witness is questioned about. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace. If the number is wrong on the top, you change it so that we have all the same numbers. I did that several times when the wrong numbers were put on Defence exhibits and it causes no problems. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do you have the entry for the 7th of December, 1992, open in front of you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does it read: "Medium level of activity today with 259 rounds incoming to Presidency side and 114 rounds incoming to Serb side."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "Total rounds recording outgoing from Serb positions, 93; from Presidency positions, 71." Now, firstly, does that illustrate the incompleteness of the UNMO recordings, in other words, they are not consistent because of difficulties that the UNMOs had in recording all shells?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It demonstrates the fact that we did not monitor all weapons on the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. The next words read: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, firstly, what is meant by those words in terms of whether the fire was understood to be against military targets or indiscriminate fire?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you must take it exactly as it is read.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Does that mean you don't know?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it means that shelling was widely dispersed throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Do you know whether that wide dispersal of fire reflected indiscriminate fire on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would indicate that not all the targets were military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. Now, I draw your attention to a further passage under that date. If you count down nine lines, the end of the ninth line has the words, "at approx." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "At approx 072000 A December, Serbs threatened to renew shelling of city if Presidency shelling of Lukavica did not cease. Presumably Serbs not satisfied with response because as of 072130 A December, Serbs have commenced shelling of city." Do you see those words?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, firstly, does 072000 A indicate the 7th of December?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. 8.00 in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And the other reference, I take it, therefore, is the 7th of December at 9.30 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Is that another example of the Serb forces threatening to shell indiscriminately the city if they did not receive what they wanted and, indeed, carrying out the threat?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please go to the following day, the 8th of December. Does that refer to "An extremely high level of activity today with 991 rounds incoming to Presidency side."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: If you go down further --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, first of all, the booth is asking the speakers to slow down. I have to make a similar request but I also have to go back to something that was mentioned at the bottom of page 80, line 25: The word "indiscriminately" does not appear in the quoted text, which makes the question a leading one, to which we have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, it is a leading question, and if you wish it to be struck out, I am happy to go back and approach it in a different way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Please go back to the entry for the 7th of December, 1992. What, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. if anything, did you understand by the threat and I now quote your words: "Serbs threatened to renew shelling of city."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their response would be a general shelling of the city, not necessarily military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you please now go to the 8th of December, 1992. I have read out the first part of the first sentence. Would you now go to the fourth line. Do these words appear: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: What did you mean by those words in terms of the nature of the targets?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was referring to specific areas of confrontation, and the "shelling widely dispersed widely throughout city" quote would relate to rounds landing in areas which were not necessarily related to those events on the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Would you now go further down the entry for that date. Would you please count down to about 12 lines, the line commencing with the letters "DSMO" in capitals?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: At the end of that line, do you see the word "indiscriminate"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do these words appear --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, once again, I have to ask the speakers to slow down, please. I can no longer take notes and it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 81.14, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...slow down is such good enough. Is there any specific issue you would like to raise apart from that?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will be happy to do so, Mr. President. The speed is such that on page 81, line 14, I was not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't want to have introductions like, "The speed was such that I could not read this." You just tell us: Page so and so, line that and that, I need a clarification. Something like that. I don't want speeches all the time. So please indicate why you have a problem and what the problem is.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We might as well continue. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Do these words appear: "Indiscriminate shelling of city intensifying"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: They do.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: And that is for the same day as the earlier words: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Are you therefore saying that the shelling --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I am really very sorry but once again I am asking the speakers to slow down because otherwise, I will -- I can just leave because I cannot perform my work. Very often, I have to verify the text which is full of mistakes. I have to react and I don't have always the time to do that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...clear that a single request for slowing down would do. And the speech you made was six lines. One line next time for complaining about the speed. Could you please slow down, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Now, the -- this indiscriminate fire that was taking place during the Otes battle or the Otes conflict, did you see any connection between the two or not?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be the reason that we would determine fire to be indiscriminate, if it bore no relation to military activity. Consequently, the fire to which you refer, which is that general fire upon the city, would be indiscriminate because there were no apparent military targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Beyond that, did you form any view as to whether there was any reasoning behind apparently, objectively, the increased incidence of indiscriminate fire and the battle going on in the western part of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: All fire that was incoming to the city of Sarajevo was analyzed along what the objective of that fire would be. If it wasn't seen to be in response to any military events, one can only assume that the indiscriminate fire was being used to fashion terror because there was no military objective.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: All right. The 9th of December, 1992, three lines down. I read the words: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city." Do those words appear?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 10th of December, three lines down: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: 11th of December, three lines down: "Shelling widely dispersed throughout city." Correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD MOLE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
